Original Research


Risk and Prognosis of Hamstring Injuries
in the National Football League
A 12-Year Review
Ryne Jenkins,*y DO, John Bianchi,y DO, Jeremy Watson,y MD, Jason Shinners,y DO,
Pooja Jaisinghani,y DO, Brett Spain,y DO, and Charles Ruotolo,y MD
Investigation performed at the Nassau University Medical Center, East Meadow, New York, USA

Background: Hamstring injuries can have a significant burden on a professional football player’s career and performance. One in
4 players will suffer a lower extremity strain in their career, with the hamstring being the most common. These injuries are often
fraught with extended periods of recovery and reinjury rates varying between 16% and 38%.
Purpose: To determine the progression and duration of hamstring injury as well as risk factors and probability of reinjury in the
National Football League (NFL).
Study Design: Descriptive epidemiology study.
Methods: Data were extracted from the official publicly accessible NFL database of injuries. NFL players suffering a hamstring
injury during the study period of 2008-2020 were identified. Injuries were reported weekly as mandated by the NFL. Players were
deemed cleared from injury when no longer listed in the injury report (IR). Reinjury was defined as any subsequent hamstring injury
after a player’s initial injury. The duration of injury and factors associated with injury were analyzed. Secondary objectives included
team-specific injury rates and timing of injury.
Results: A total of 2101 hamstring injuries occurred among 1354 players. The mean duration of the IR was 2.4 6 2.1 weeks. A
total of 442 (33%) players suffered subsequent reinjury, 27% of which occurred during the same season. The mean duration on
the IR for reinjury was 2.4 6 1.8 weeks, with no significant difference in duration compared with initial injury (2.4 6 1.8 vs 2.2 6
1.7; P = .138). Defensive skill players were most frequently injured (50.4%) followed by offensive skill players (37.7%). Of the 4812
total IR listings, 1806 (38%) did not participate in practice. A total of 1590 (33.5%) had limited participation in practice, and 1353
(28.5%) had full participation in practice. Injury rates among teams varied and ranged from 0.6% (Baltimore Ravens) to 5.7%
(Houston Texans), with a median of 3.1% (P \ .0001).
Conclusion: Hamstring injuries can have a lasting impact on a player’s career with more than a third of players suffering subse-
quent reinjury. Although suffering a hamstring injury predisposes a player to reinjury, previous injury was not associated with lon-
ger recovery times. Rates of injury among organizational teams vary; thus, further research to understand the difference in
preventive measures and treatment protocols may be warranted.
Keywords: football (American); hamstring injury; hamstring strain; injury prevention; National Football League; physical
therapy/rehabilitation

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file
entries.description:
Read a file into a sandboxed FILE_CONTENT variable and run code over it. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation — the file bytes stay in the sandbox.

Think-in-Code applied to file-level analysis: Reading the whole file means every byte enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. Running code over it here lets you keep the raw bytes out and only the derived answer in. Same principle as ctx_execute, scoped to one named file via the FILE_CONTENT variable.

WHEN:
  - You want to KNOW SOMETHING ABOUT a file (line count, matches of a pattern, parsed structure, statistical aggregate) without needing to SEE all of it
  - The file is structured (CSV, JSON, log, code) and a code-level derivation is cheaper than reading verbatim
  - The file is large enough that reading the full content would burn meaningful conversation memory you need for the actual work
  - The derivation may itself produce a large output you want recall-by-topic on later — pass an `intent` string; outputs over ~5KB are auto-indexed and only matching sections come back, retrievable via ctx_search

WHEN NOT:
  - You intend to EDIT the file — use Read so the subsequent Edit can match the exact text
  - You only need one specific line and you know its offset — Read with offset/limit is the simplest path
  - The file is small AND you will consume all of it for understanding/editing — Read directly

RETURNS:
  Only what your code prints. The FILE_CONTENT variable holds the raw bytes inside the sandbox; nothing else leaves. When `intent` is set and output exceeds the auto-index threshold, the response carries searchable section titles + previews instead of the raw stdout.

EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "huge.log", language: "javascript", code: "const errs = FILE_CONTENT.split('\\n').filter(l => /ERROR|FATAL/.test(l)); console.log(`${errs.length} error lines`); console.log(errs.slice(-5).join('\\n'))")
EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "data.csv", language: "javascript", code: "const rows = FILE_CONTENT.split('\\n'); console.log(`rows: ${rows.length - 1}, header: ${rows[0]}`)")

path.description: Absolute file path or relative to project root

code.description: Code to process FILE_CONTENT (file_content in Elixir). Print summary via console.log/print/echo/IO.puts/Console.WriteLine.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs.

intent.description: What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), returns only matching sections via BM25 search instead of truncated output.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-index call), then come back here to query
  - You have one ad-hoc question against data that is not in the knowledge base — answer it inline by running code in the sandbox tool; one round-trip instead of capture-then-query

RETURNS:
  Per-query ranked sections with window-extracted snippets. Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query. Common session-memory source labels: `decision` (user corrections / preferences), `error` and `error-resolution` (past failures + their fixes), `blocker`, `plan`, `user-prompt`, `rejected-approach`, `compaction` (post-compact session guide). See ctx_stats for live category counts. Each response carries a throttle counter (call #N/M in the rolling time window); results taper toward the soft cap and calls block after the hard cap. Tune via CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_WINDOW_MS, CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS_AFTER, CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_BLOCK_AFTER.

EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix", "test coverage"], source: "issue-#683")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["what did we decide about caching"], source: "decision", sort: "timeline")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["useEffect cleanup pattern"], source: "react-docs", contentType: "code", limit: 5)
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["last user prompt", "active skills", "open blockers"], sort: "timeline")

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

project.description: Project scope. Default (omit): this session's project — auto-resolved from the host adapter. 'global': span every project in the shared store (cross-project recall). <absolute-path>: scope to that specific project directory.

120	Medical provider’s ability to detect, diagnose, and treat sport-related concussion (SRC) has
121

123	
124	involved in concussion, it is still uncertain whether there are preventative measures athletes can
125	
126	take to prevent a SRC from occurring. The objective of this review was to determine if either
127

129

157

181	 Introduction
182	
183	       Though there is no universally accepted definition of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI),
184	
185	it is generally defined as an acute brain injury resulting from mechanical energy to the head from
186	
187	external physical forces1, 2. Diagnostic criteria include loss of consciousness less than 30
188	
189	minutes, post traumatic amnesia less than 24 hours, a Glascow Coma Scale score of 13 to 152, as
190	
191	well as mental status and behavioral changes, and/or neurological signs 3. Though the clinical
192	
193	
194	                                                                           D
195	presentation of mTBI can vary, often the terms mTBI and concussion are used interchangeably3.
196	
197	Of particular interest in the athletic population is sport-related concussion (SRC). SRC is defined
198	
199	
200	
201	
202	                           EP
203	as brain injury resulting in the disturbance of typical brain functioning and involves a complex
204	
205	pathophysiological process4-6. SRC incidence is estimated to be around 3.8 million injuries per
206	
207	
208	
209	
210	                             TE
211	year in the United States7. At the high-school level, the incidence rate of SRCs is highest in
212	
213	boys’ football (10.40 per 10,000 athletic exposures [AEs]), followed by girls’ soccer (8.19 per
214	
215	10,000 AEs) and boys’ ice hockey (7.69 per 10,000 AEs)8. SRCs can also occur at all levels of
216	
217	low contact sports (e.g. tennis, swimming, track and field). The true incidence of SRC is likely
218	
219	higher than documented, as many athletes may not recognize or report their SRC9-11. Notably,
220	
221	             C
222	the Center for Disease Control and Prevention claims that five out of ten concussions go
223	
224	undiagnosed or undetected12.
225	
226	 C
227	A      The biomechanical forces involved in concussion include direct impact to the head, or an
228	
229	impact to another part of the body with a mechanical force transmitted to the head13. These
230	
231	forces can be linear or rotational14. In addition to increased acceleration, the direction of
232	
233	acceleration is also important, as head impacts in the real world occur in all planes of motion.
234	
235	There is evidence to suggest that coronal plane acceleration (lateral flexion) may be more
236	
237	
238	
239	
240	                                                        4
241	
242	       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
243	 injurious than sagittal plane acceleration (flexion and extension)15. Ultimately, a better
244	
245	understanding of the biomechanical forces that cause concussion may lead to more targeted
246	
247	prevention approaches.
248	
249	
250

252	
253	improved, the ability to prevent SRCs from occurring and decrease the severity of clinical
254	
255

257	outcomes post-injury is limited16. If the acceleration of the brain during an impact can be
258

260	
261	
262	
263

265	important concept as the greatest opportunity to impact overall injury burden often lies in injury
266	
267	prevention14. However, the literature is sparse in regard to concussion prevention in athletes.

276

278

280

282

285	
286

290	
291	in other team sports specifically targeting exercise components aimed to reduce concussion rates,
292

297	
298	rates is recommended)17, none of the recommendations included cervical strength. Four of the
299	
300	recommendations were specific to a singular sport and the fifth was a general comment about
301	
302	policy change17. Thus, there are no agreed upon guidelines or formal recommendations in regard
303	
304	to cervical strength or cervical strengthening programs and athlete concussion reduction.
305	
306	
307	
308	
309	                                                        5
310	
311	       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
312	        Neck size and neck strength have emerged as modifiable characteristics associated with
313	
314	concussion risk12, 14. Neck size is an easily measured variable given that neck circumference can
315	
316	be obtained with simple and accessible tools, like a measuring tape. Isometric neck strength,
317	
318	though a more difficult variable to test due to the need for equipment, such as a dynamometer,
319	
320	may be more clinically useful because it is a more functional characteristic as opposed to neck
321	
322	size alone, which is static measurement. There also may be certain athlete populations that could
323	
324

326	benefit from a formal cervical strengthening program, since they have weaker necks18, 19,
327

329	
330

337

351

354

359	
360	area spread across a variety of sports and athlete populations, the inclusion criteria was
361	
362

365	intentionally kept broad to ensure we captured the literature available on the topic. All articles
366	
367	relating to sports related concussion and neck size and/or neck strength were included, regardless
368	
369	of the sport, gender of the athletes, or age of the athletes. The primary author reviewed the
370

381	 this manuscript. Combining the 20 articles from Google Scholar and 13 articles from Ovid
382	
383	MEDLINE resulted in a total of 33 articles included for this literature review (Figure 1).
384	
385	
386	
387	Discussion
388	
389	Neck Size
390	
391	       Neck size, typically measured as neck circumference, was theorized to be a protective
392	
393	
394	                                                                           D
395	factor for concussion, as a larger neck could mechanically resist more force and prevent a
396	
397	concussion from occurring. Neck circumference has been proposed as a simple proxy measure of
398	
399	
400	
401	
402	                           EP
403	other features of the cervical spine, such as neck strength20. However, the literature does not
404	
405	support this theory. Neck circumference has not been shown to be related to SRC history or
406	
407	
408	
409	
410	                             TE
411	subsequent SRC. Since neck size is not related to SRC, additional studies examined proportional
412	
413	neck circumference (neck circumference in proportion to body mass)20. Similarly, there was no
414	
415	relationship to proportional neck circumference and reduction of SRC. Males had a significantly
416	
417	larger neck circumference and proportional neck circumference compared to females, but when
418	
419	controlling for sex, there was no association between neck circumference and SRC20. Eckner et
420	
421	             C
422	al. found possible evidence that increased neck size may correlate with reduced concussion risk
423	
424	in high-school aged male athletes involved in contact or collision sports21. Their results showed
425	
426	  C
427	that neck girth, quantified by measuring the circumference of the neck at the level of the thyroid
428	
429

     Risk Reduction of Concussion in Athletes: Do Neck Size or Neck Strength

                                                 Make a Difference?




     Sean Silverman, DO1, Meghan E. Vidt, PhD1,2, Justin S. Hong, MD1, Lori M. Grafton, MD1



1

A

relationships related to the enclosed work that may lead to bias or a conflict of interest.

analyzed.

 Ethics Disclosure: This work is a review article. As no human or animal subjects were

examined as a part of this study, no ethics board approval was required.



Author Contribution Statement:

Sean Silverman, DO: conceptualization, methodology, investigation, resources, writing,

review/editing, visualization. Meghan E. Vidt, PhD: methodology, investigation, resources,


                                                                           D
review/editing, visualization, supervision. Justin S. Hong, MD: review/editing, supervision.

Lori M. Grafton, MD: review/editing, supervision.



Corresponding Author:
                           EP
Meghan E. Vidt, PhD



                             TE
331 Chemical and Biomedical Engineering Building

Pennsylvania State University

University Park, PA 16802, USA

Phone: 814-865-6885

             C
Fax: 814-863-0490



 C
Email: mzv130@psu.edu




A

Sean Silverman is in training.




                                                        2

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Abstract

Medical provider’s ability to detect, diagnose, and treat sport-related concussion (SRC) has

greatly improved in recent years. Though more is known about the biomechanical forces

involved in concussion, it is still uncertain whether there are preventative measures athletes can

take to prevent a SRC from occurring. The objective of this review was to determine if either

neck size or neck strength is related to a decreased risk of sustaining a SRC. A literature review


                                                                           D
was conducted on Google Scholar and Ovid MEDLINE for pertinent articles. Findings indicate

that isometric neck strength, but not neck size, has been shown to be a predictor for SRC




                           EP
prevention. Formal neck strengthening programs are feasible and lead to decreased SRC risk.

Additionally, there may be greater opportunity to increase neck strength in amateur athletes




                             TE
compared to professional. In conclusion, cervical strengthening programs have been shown to be

feasible and beneficial for athletes to decrease their risk of sustaining a SRC, though the optimal

duration, intensity, and frequency has yet to be determined.



Keywords: brain concussion, concussion, primary prevention, neck strengthening, cervical

strengtheningC
 C
List of Abbreviations

mTBI, Mild Traumatic Brain Injury



A
SRC, Sport-related concussion

AE, athletic exposure

U18, under age 18

FIFA 11 +, Federation Internationale de Football Association’s 11+ Injury Prevention Program




                                                        3

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Introduction

       Though there is no universally accepted definition of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI),

it is generally defined as an acute brain injury resulting from mechanical energy to the head from

external physical forces1, 2. Diagnostic criteria include loss of consciousness less than 30

minutes, post traumatic amnesia less than 24 hours, a Glascow Coma Scale score of 13 to 152, as

well as mental status and behavioral changes, and/or neurological signs 3. Though the clinical


                                                                           D
presentation of mTBI can vary, often the terms mTBI and concussion are used interchangeably3.

Of particular interest in the athletic population is sport-related concussion (SRC). SRC is defined




                           EP
as brain injury resulting in the disturbance of typical brain functioning and involves a complex

pathophysiological process4-6. SRC incidence is estimated to be around 3.8 million injuries per




                             TE
year in the United States7. At the high-school level, the incidence rate of SRCs is highest in

boys’ football (10.40 per 10,000 athletic exposures [AEs]), followed by girls’ soccer (8.19 per

10,000 AEs) and boys’ ice hockey (7.69 per 10,000 AEs)8. SRCs can also occur at all levels of

low contact sports (e.g. tennis, swimming, track and field). The true incidence of SRC is likely

higher than documented, as many athletes may not recognize or report their SRC9-11. Notably,

             C
the Center for Disease Control and Prevention claims that five out of ten concussions go

undiagnosed or undetected12.

 C
A      The biomechanical forces involved in concussion include direct impact to the head, or an

impact to another part of the body with a mechanical force transmitted to the head13. These

forces can be linear or rotational14. In addition to increased acceleration, the direction of

acceleration is also important, as head impacts in the real world occur in all planes of motion.

There is evidence to suggest that coronal plane acceleration (lateral flexion) may be more




                                                        4

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 injurious than sagittal plane acceleration (flexion and extension)15. Ultimately, a better

understanding of the biomechanical forces that cause concussion may lead to more targeted

prevention approaches.



       Although the medical community’s ability to detect, diagnose, and treat SRC has greatly

improved, the ability to prevent SRCs from occurring and decrease the severity of clinical


                                                                           D
outcomes post-injury is limited16. If the acceleration of the brain during an impact can be

decreased14, it has been theorized that this could prevent a concussion from occurring. This is an




                           EP
important concept as the greatest opportunity to impact overall injury burden often lies in injury

prevention14. However, the literature is sparse in regard to concussion prevention in athletes.




                             TE
Patricios et al. has recently published a revised consensus statement on concussion in sport.

While there were five unanimously-supported recommendations for concussion prevention (i:

Mouthguard use should be supported in child and adolescent ice hockey, ii: Policy disallowing

body checking should be supported for all children and most levels of adolescent ice hockey, iii:

Strategies limiting contact practice in American football should inform related policies and

             C
recommendations for all levels, iv: neuromuscular training warm-up programmes are



 C
recommended, based on research in rugby, and more research is needed for female athletes and

in other team sports specifically targeting exercise components aimed to reduce concussion rates,



A
v: Policy supporting optimal concussion management strategies to reduce recurrent concussion

rates is recommended)17, none of the recommendations included cervical strength. Four of the

recommendations were specific to a singular sport and the fifth was a general comment about

policy change17. Thus, there are no agreed upon guidelines or formal recommendations in regard

to cervical strength or cervical strengthening programs and athlete concussion reduction.




                                                        5

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
        Neck size and neck strength have emerged as modifiable characteristics associated with

concussion risk12, 14. Neck size is an easily measured variable given that neck circumference can

be obtained with simple and accessible tools, like a measuring tape. Isometric neck strength,

though a more difficult variable to test due to the need for equipment, such as a dynamometer,

may be more clinically useful because it is a more functional characteristic as opposed to neck

size alone, which is static measurement. There also may be certain athlete populations that could


                                                                           D
benefit from a formal cervical strengthening program, since they have weaker necks18, 19,

including amateur athletes and female athletes. Due to the paucity of research and data on this




                           EP
topic, the purpose of this narrative review is to examine all the literature available regarding neck

size and/or neck strength and its relation to SRC prevention and if a formal cervical strength




                             TE
training program decreases SRCs.



Methods

       A search of Ovid MEDLINE database was performed with the key terms outlined in box

A, resulting in 13 articles. Google Scholar was utilized to search for additional articles with key

             C
terms outlined in box B, resulting in 552 articles. An additional filter to exclude articles prior to



  C
the year 2000 was used, which resulted in 485 articles. As there is a paucity of research in this

area spread across a variety of sports and athlete populations, the inclusion criteria was



A
intentionally kept broad to ensure we captured the literature available on the topic. All articles

relating to sports related concussion and neck size and/or neck strength were included, regardless

of the sport, gender of the athletes, or age of the athletes. The primary author reviewed the

remaining 485 articles and included all 22 articles related to sports related concussion. Two

articles were later removed during the article revision process as they were outside the scope of




                                                        6

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 this manuscript. Combining the 20 articles from Google Scholar and 13 articles from Ovid

MEDLINE resulted in a total of 33 articles included for this literature review (Figure 1).



Discussion

Neck Size

       Neck size, typically measured as neck circumference, was theorized to be a protective


                                                                           D
factor for concussion, as a larger neck could mechanically resist more force and prevent a

concussion from occurring. Neck circumference has been proposed as a simple proxy measure of




                           EP
other features of the cervical spine, such as neck strength20. However, the literature does not

support this theory. Neck circumference has not been shown to be related to SRC history or




                             TE
subsequent SRC. Since neck size is not related to SRC, additional studies examined proportional

neck circumference (neck circumference in proportion to body mass)20. Similarly, there was no

relationship to proportional neck circumference and reduction of SRC. Males had a significantly

larger neck circumference and proportional neck circumference compared to females, but when

controlling for sex, there was no association between neck circumference and SRC20. Eckner et

             C
al. found possible evidence that increased neck size may correlate with reduced concussion risk

in high-school aged male athletes involved in contact or collision sports21. Their results showed

  C
that neck girth, quantified by measuring the circumference of the neck at the level of the thyroid



A
cartilage, was associated with decreased SRC but only with an increase in isometric neck

strength. Collectively, larger neck girth was only associated with decreased SRC if there was

also a concomitant increase in isometric neck strength. There were also findings that an increase

in neck strength without a change in neck girth also led to decreased concussion risk, but the

opposite was not true21. One must be cautious when simply attributing neck circumference to




                                                        7

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 decreased risk of SRC after a cervical strengthening program, as it appears the more pertinent

variable is neck strength. Eckner et al. has suggested a theory that initial strengthening may not

lead to significant changes in neck size, but significant changes in strength. This theory is

consistent with the effect of weight lifting regimes on extremity muscles, where initial strength

gains are from neural adaptation rather than muscle hypertrophy21.



Isometric Neck Strength
                                                                           D
       There is markedly more evidence showing that isometric neck strength is a protective




                           EP
factor from SRC. Cervical musculature is primarily responsible for maintaining posture and

stabilizing the head at rest22. Cervical muscle contraction is theorized to more rigidly couple the




                             TE
head to the torso, and therefore decrease the acceleration experienced by the brain14. Neck

stiffness, via the cervical musculature, is the dynamic ability of the neck to reduce translational

head displacement, velocity, and acceleration15. Individuals who have stronger necks can more

effectively distribute potentially injurious forces from impacts compared to those with weaker

necks23. Greater neck strength has been shown to decrease acceleration of the head during rugby

             C
contact events24. In particular, the sternocleidomastoid muscle has been shown to be the single



 C
muscle making the greatest contribution to force generation across all planes of cervical spine

motion21. Head position at impact can also result in greater forces to the brain. Forward head



A
posture is defined as the external auditory meatus being positioned anterior to the glenohumeral

with weaker neck strength were more likely to suffer concussion, and that females had weaker

necks compared to males27. Peek et al. found similar results whereby female collegiate soccer




                             TE
players exhibited significantly lower neck strength and greater head accelerations during

purposeful heading than males25. In the future, literature will need to address these differences

between the sexes. In order to prevent SRC there may need to be specific exercises tailored

toward males and females. For example, Daly et al. concluded there must be a more

comprehensive understanding of the etiology of concussion in females13 because not only are

             C
females more at risk for SRC, but they report greater symptom severity and longer recovery



 C
times than males. Striefer et al. had similar findings, showing that females experienced more

severe symptoms and longer recovery patterns post-SRC than males16. The fact that females



A
suffer concussion at a greater rate and have more significant symptoms with prolonged recovery

times compared to males highlight the importance of identifying and implementing preventative

measures to offset SRC risk. Although the literature is currently sparse, there is emerging

evidence that neck strengthening exercises can help offset risk of experiencing SRC. Prior work

shows that females achieved greater relative strength increases than males following a




                                                       16

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 strengthening regimen, suggesting that the degree of disparity can be reduced19. It has been

hypothesized that females have greater neuromuscular activation to account for their lower neck

strength, which could be one possible mechanism female athletes may rely on for concussion

prevention23. Ultimately, there appears to be a disparity between males and females in regard to

SRC occurrence. This may prove clinically important in the future, as treatment and preventative

measures may also differ between the sexes.



Conclusion and Limitations
                                                                           D
                           EP
       Concussion management has centered around treatment after the injury has occurred, but

it is well known in medicine that injury prevention is the ultimate goal. Primary prevention in




                             TE
regard to SRC is in its infancy, but has some emerging topics. At the forefront is neck or cervical

characteristics, which may serve as protective indicators. However, the evidence to support neck

circumference or size as a protective factor is still lacking. Though an easily measurable trait

with a possibility for a quick screening tool, increased neck size has not yet shown any

relationship to concussion prevention. On the contrary, neck strength does have supportive

             C
evidence to be a protective factor against concussion. More importantly, it has been shown that a



 C
simple neck isometric strengthening program is able to increase neck strength and decrease

concussion risk. However, caution must be exercised as strengthening programs appear to be



A
most helpful in certain populations, like females achieving greater benefit than males, and

amateurs compared to professionals. Similarly, due to the functional and anatomical differences

between the sexes, different exercise programs tailored to sex are needed. It is also unclear if a

cervical strengthening program would benefit athletes in all sports, and the duration, intensity,

and frequency of a cervical strengthening program has yet to be determined.

297	3.1 Study selection and characteristics
298	From eight databases, the online search returned 4,012 records, of which 1,291 duplicates
299	were removed. See Figure 1 for PRISMA screening process results. Of the 2,721 remaining,
300	17 papers [61-77] fit the inclusion criteria and were included for review. The characteristics
301	of each study are described in Table 2. Nine different sports were represented in the
302	seventeen studies which included lacrosse [62, 63, 73], soccer [61-68, 70-74], field hockey
303	[62, 63], football (American) [69, 76], Rugby league [75], Rugby union [75], Australian rules
304	football [75], Gaelic football [77], and hurling [77]. The modified CASP assessment is
305	presented in Supplementary Table 1.
306	
307	3.2 Injury surveillance
308	In terms of method of diagnosis, one study confirmed ankle sprains by MRI [75], with eight
309	using assessment by a medical physician [62-64, 66, 68, 72, 74, 77], two using ‘medical staff
310	or personnel’ [67, 71], one using a ‘certified athletic trainer or physician’ [69], and five did
311	not acknowledge confirmation or means of diagnosis [61, 65, 70, 73, 76]. In relation to injury
312	recording, nine studies described their protocol for maintaining injury records [61, 64, 65, 67-
313	70, 75, 76] of which six were maintained by the medical staff as part of the original
314	diagnoses. One study appointed undergraduate students [71], and one had the players
315	themselves maintain their own records [77]. Six studies were unclear in reporting these
316	methods [62, 63, 66, 71, 73, 74]. The incidence rate (no. of sprains / exposure) was not
317	described in ten of the studies [62, 65-69, 71, 72, 76, 77]. From the seven studies that did
318	report overall incidence rate, three studies represented data in (#) sprains/1000 hours:
319	0.6/1000 h [61], 0.36/1000 h [64], 0.47/1000 h [67], 2.16/1000 h [70], and 0.89/1000 h
320	(Rugby union) & 0.46/1000 h (Rugby league) [75]; with one describing in (#) sprains/person-
321	days (p-d), 1.6/1000 p-d (males) & 2.2/1000 p-d (females) [63] and one reported ankle
322	sprains per 10,000 player exposures (12.8 /10,000 AEs) [73].
323	
324	Among the seventeen studies included, four studies did not differentiate between types of
325	sprain (LAS, MAS, HAS) or mechanism of injury (i.e. contact vs non-contact) [61, 65, 66,
326	77]; six investigated inversion sprains only [62-64, 68, 69, 71], while three investigated
327	inversion sprains but excluded contact mechanisms [73, 74, 76]. Additionally, one study
328	investigated only syndesmosis sprains [75]; and two studies reported non-contact mechanism
329	only (no differentiation for type of ankle sprain) [67, 69], of which one reported only LAS in
330	their results [67]. Kofotolis et al. [70] reported ankle sprains by individual ligaments rather
331	than the anatomical region, as well as reported contact and non-contact sprains.
332	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                             7
333	
334	
335	Four studies investigated the grades of ankle sprains [62, 63, 66, 76], two of which reported
336	the results [62, 76]. Baumhauer et al. [62] reported 12 Grade-I, 3 Grade-II, and 0 Grade-III
337	injuries from a total of 15 inversion sprains in their study. Among the 15 diagnosed non-
338	contact sprains reported by Tyler et al. [76], 11 were Grade-I, 3 were Grade-II, and 1 was a
339	Grade-III sprain. Severity defined by time-loss was represented in three papers [64, 68, 70].

850	                                        4 DISCUSSION
851	4.1 Summary of Main Findings
852	This study is the first review of ankle sprain risk factors measured in a comprehensive list of
853	field-based, team contact sports. Data from the seventeen studies included in the review came
854	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   19
855	
856	
857	from nine different sports including the sports of lacrosse, soccer, field hockey, American
858	football, rugby league, rugby union, Australian rules football, Gaelic football, and hurling. In
859	total, twenty different categories were assessed as potential risk factors, twelve of which
860	showed an association to ankle sprain incidence [63]. Deficits or asymmetries in ankle
861	strength [62, 67] and hip strength [64, 74], and greater BMI [67, 76] were all associated with
862	an increased likelihood of sustaining an ankle sprain in two different studies each, with single
863	leg landing performance outcomes [68, 73] and single leg anterior reach associated in others
864	[69]. Height [71] and mass [67] were independently associated with ankle sprain risk in other
865	cohorts. Finally, joint laxity was associated with ankle sprain incidence in one study [63]
866	while anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle represented as a risk factor in two different
867	studies [62, 63].
868	
869	4.2 Comparison to Existing Literature
870	Injury events in sport will involve differing kinematics and kinetics thus affecting different
871	anatomical structures [78]. While ankle sprain prevalence across sports has been established,
872	further epidemiological dissection of specific ankle sprain etiology is needed. Varying grades
873	of ankle sprain have previously been defined to aid different treatment strategies [79]. Indeed,
874	diagnosing sprains by grade is one way to categorize severity; but it would prove more
875	beneficial for coaches and medical staff to additionally communicate the impact through
876	estimated time-loss to relevant stakeholders during the course of a season, rather than the
877	architectural state of injured structures [22]. While injury severity (time-loss) is a calculation
878	made retrospectively at the end of a season, only three studies in this review reported average
879	time-loss per ankle sprain [64, 68, 70]. Furthermore, Bahr et al. have suggested there is a
880	need for sport injury epidemiological studies to report injury burden (combining injury
881	severity and incidence rate) to better manage overall risk in the sporting setting [80].
882	
883	4.3 Injury Surveillance
884	For prospectively defining injury, nine studies included time-loss as part of their injury
885	definition, with two studies having required at least a week of absence [74, 77], one required
886	a modified [75] and two required missed [67, 76] game or practice. Two others specified 1
887	day of missed sport activity [69, 71], one at least 48 hours of missed participation [64], and
888	one noted ‘time-loss’ with no specified time window [72]. In order to continue evolving from
889	epidemiological studies to etiological studies, practitioners and researchers should
890	standardize records and reports according to consensus statements published for many sports
891	[81-85], including the most recent consensus statement by the International Olympic
892	Committee [86].
893	
894	4.4 Anthropometric Risk Factors
895	Anthropometric assessments were the most commonly measured category across the
896	seventeen studies. From the ten studies that measured BMI as an independent risk factor,
897	effect sizes varied from medium to large. While De Ridder et al. [64] reported a higher BMI
898	as a significant risk factor with a large effect size, and Fousekis et al. [67] an 8-fold increase
899	in ankle sprain risk for a BMI above the sample median, Watson et al. [77] on the other hand
900	found a negative relationship suggesting that a higher BMI may be protective against ankle
901	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   20
902	
903	
904	sprains. The findings of Watson et al. [77] should be considered with caution as the type of
905	ankle sprains were not reported in their inclusion nor exclusion criteria, and there was a lack
906	of clarity reported in the methods section of this study as evident in CASP assessment. A
907	higher BMI as indicative of risk, similar to the results of De Ridder et al. [64] and Fousekis et
908	al. [67] has also been found previously for general lower extremity injury [87]. It is worth
909	noting that the methods used to measure BMI differed across studies, that is, three studies
910	were vague in their methods of recording mass and height [64, 76, 77], two used a
911	standardized physician scale [67, 71], one did not acknowledge these methods [74], and four
912	utilized self-reporting [62, 63, 69, 75]. This non-invasive recall method does provide a way of
913	saving practitioners time in team settings, while also showing good reliability in recent
914	studies [88], but it would not be considered the gold standard. An additional body size
915	classification (BW x HT2) was investigated originally by Milgrom et al. [89], and found
916	positive association for ankle sprain incidence in military recruits. Similarly, De Ridder et al.
917	[64] showed statistical significance and a large effect size when comparing the injured and
918	uninjured groups in their study. Therefore, further studies are warranted to include this
919	adjusted body size in their methods as a potential risk factor for ankle sprains.
920	
921	4.5 Foot and Ankle Risk Factors
922	Anatomical alignment of the foot and ankle as measured by a goniometer was associated with
923	increased risk of injury in two studies [62, 63]. Dorsiflexion range of motion was considered
924	as a factor for risk in three studies [67, 75, 77], but results were reported in only one [75].
925	Sman et al. [75] used the weight-bearing lunge test which has shown to have ‘good’ inter-
926	and intra-tester reliability, while also showing efficacy for time, space and cost. However,
927	they reported no relationship and a small effect size (Cohen’s d= -.121) between the injured
928	group and uninjured group for dorsiflexion, therefore more evidence is needed to include
929	dorsiflexion as a risk factor. Two [62, 67] of the four [62, 63, 67, 75] studies which measured
930	ankle strength as a risk factor found significant differences between groups. Baumhauer et al.

4 DISCUSSION
4.1 Summary of Main Findings
This study is the first review of ankle sprain risk factors measured in a comprehensive list of
field-based, team contact sports. Data from the seventeen studies included in the review came
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   19


from nine different sports including the sports of lacrosse, soccer, field hockey, American
football, rugby league, rugby union, Australian rules football, Gaelic football, and hurling. In
total, twenty different categories were assessed as potential risk factors, twelve of which
showed an association to ankle sprain incidence [63]. Deficits or asymmetries in ankle
strength [62, 67] and hip strength [64, 74], and greater BMI [67, 76] were all associated with
an increased likelihood of sustaining an ankle sprain in two different studies each, with single
leg landing performance outcomes [68, 73] and single leg anterior reach associated in others
[69]. Height [71] and mass [67] were independently associated with ankle sprain risk in other
cohorts. Finally, joint laxity was associated with ankle sprain incidence in one study [63]
while anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle represented as a risk factor in two different
studies [62, 63].

4.2 Comparison to Existing Literature
Injury events in sport will involve differing kinematics and kinetics thus affecting different
anatomical structures [78]. While ankle sprain prevalence across sports has been established,
further epidemiological dissection of specific ankle sprain etiology is needed. Varying grades
of ankle sprain have previously been defined to aid different treatment strategies [79]. Indeed,
diagnosing sprains by grade is one way to categorize severity; but it would prove more
beneficial for coaches and medical staff to additionally communicate the impact through
estimated time-loss to relevant stakeholders during the course of a season, rather than the
architectural state of injured structures [22]. While injury severity (time-loss) is a calculation
made retrospectively at the end of a season, only three studies in this review reported average
time-loss per ankle sprain [64, 68, 70]. Furthermore, Bahr et al. have suggested there is a
need for sport injury epidemiological studies to report injury burden (combining injury
severity and incidence rate) to better manage overall risk in the sporting setting [80].

4.3 Injury Surveillance
For prospectively defining injury, nine studies included time-loss as part of their injury
definition, with two studies having required at least a week of absence [74, 77], one required
a modified [75] and two required missed [67, 76] game or practice. Two others specified 1
day of missed sport activity [69, 71], one at least 48 hours of missed participation [64], and
one noted ‘time-loss’ with no specified time window [72]. In order to continue evolving from
epidemiological studies to etiological studies, practitioners and researchers should
standardize records and reports according to consensus statements published for many sports
[81-85], including the most recent consensus statement by the International Olympic
Committee [86].

4.4 Anthropometric Risk Factors
Anthropometric assessments were the most commonly measured category across the
seventeen studies. From the ten studies that measured BMI as an independent risk factor,
effect sizes varied from medium to large. While De Ridder et al. [64] reported a higher BMI
as a significant risk factor with a large effect size, and Fousekis et al. [67] an 8-fold increase
in ankle sprain risk for a BMI above the sample median, Watson et al. [77] on the other hand
found a negative relationship suggesting that a higher BMI may be protective against ankle
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   20


sprains. The findings of Watson et al. [77] should be considered with caution as the type of
ankle sprains were not reported in their inclusion nor exclusion criteria, and there was a lack
of clarity reported in the methods section of this study as evident in CASP assessment. A
higher BMI as indicative of risk, similar to the results of De Ridder et al. [64] and Fousekis et
al. [67] has also been found previously for general lower extremity injury [87]. It is worth
noting that the methods used to measure BMI differed across studies, that is, three studies
were vague in their methods of recording mass and height [64, 76, 77], two used a
standardized physician scale [67, 71], one did not acknowledge these methods [74], and four
utilized self-reporting [62, 63, 69, 75]. This non-invasive recall method does provide a way of
saving practitioners time in team settings, while also showing good reliability in recent
studies [88], but it would not be considered the gold standard. An additional body size
classification (BW x HT2) was investigated originally by Milgrom et al. [89], and found
positive association for ankle sprain incidence in military recruits. Similarly, De Ridder et al.
[64] showed statistical significance and a large effect size when comparing the injured and
uninjured groups in their study. Therefore, further studies are warranted to include this
adjusted body size in their methods as a potential risk factor for ankle sprains.

4.5 Foot and Ankle Risk Factors
Anatomical alignment of the foot and ankle as measured by a goniometer was associated with
increased risk of injury in two studies [62, 63]. Dorsiflexion range of motion was considered
as a factor for risk in three studies [67, 75, 77], but results were reported in only one [75].
Sman et al. [75] used the weight-bearing lunge test which has shown to have ‘good’ inter-
and intra-tester reliability, while also showing efficacy for time, space and cost. However,
they reported no relationship and a small effect size (Cohen’s d= -.121) between the injured
group and uninjured group for dorsiflexion, therefore more evidence is needed to include
dorsiflexion as a risk factor. Two [62, 67] of the four [62, 63, 67, 75] studies which measured
ankle strength as a risk factor found significant differences between groups. Baumhauer et al.
[62] found that between groups, the ratio of concentric eversion:inversion strength was higher
in the injured group, and showed a medium effect size (Cohen’s d= 0.52). The same study
reported bilateral values within the injured player, finding statistically significant differences
but small effect sizes between the injured and uninjured limb in concentric plantarflexion
(Cohen’s d= 0.18) and the ratio of concentric dorsiflexion:plantarflexion (Cohen’s d= -.39).
Fousekis at al. [67] reported an 8.88 odds ratio for those with a 15% or greater asymmetry in
eccentric dorsiflexion and eccentric plantarflexion strength. In an investigation of 241 male
physical education students, Willems et al. [90] showed that decreased concentric
dorsiflexion strength relative to body mass was also associated with inversion sprains. When

{

 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text, 'Risk and Prognosis of Hamstring Injuries in the National Football League: A 12-Year Review', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Other",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Descriptive epidemiology study of weekly NFL injury report listings for hamstring injuries over 12 seasons from the public NFL database. It identified 2101 hamstring injuries in 1354 players, and 442 players (33%) had at least one reinjury. Mean time on the injury report was 2.4 weeks, and reinjuries were not longer than first injuries (2.4 vs 2.2 weeks, P = .138).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Public injury-report data omit preseason injuries, tear severity, imaging and treatment, and cover elite players only, so results may not transfer to lower levels. Team injury rates are shares of listings rather than exposure-adjusted, and the descriptive design cannot show causes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the team-to-team injury-rate differences (0.6% to 5.7% of listings) as evidence that some organizations' prevention or treatment works, when the data cannot show exposure, programs or causes.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2024,
  "citation":"Jenkins R, Bianchi J, Watson J, Shinners J, Jaisinghani P, Spain B, et al. Risk and Prognosis of Hamstring Injuries in the National Football League: A 12-Year Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2024;12(12):23259671241298622.",
  "doi":"10.1177/23259671241298622",
  "abstract":"This descriptive study used public NFL injury report data to examine hamstring injuries over 12 seasons. About one third of players were reinjured, and team-level injury rates varied widely. The authors suggest further research into why preventive measures and treatment protocols differ between organizations.",
  "tldr":"NFL hamstring injuries kept players out about 2.4 weeks on average, and about one third of injured players were reinjured. Staff should plan for reinjury risk, but this database cannot explain why some teams have more injuries.",
  "methods":"Weekly NFL injury report listings for hamstring injuries were extracted from the public NFL database for 12 seasons. Time on the injury report, practice and game status, position, team rates and reinjury were summarized with descriptive statistics, t tests and chi-square tests.",
  "findings":"There were 2101 hamstring injuries in 1354 players, and 442 players (33%) had a reinjury. Defensive skill players accounted for 50.4% of injuries, and linebackers had the highest share at 20.1%. Previous injury was not associated with a longer time on the injury report.",
  "limitations":"Only in-season listings were used, preseason injuries are not in the database, and tear severity, imaging and treatment are not reported. Data come from elite players with dedicated rehabilitation staff. The abstract gives the study period as 2008 to 2020, while the Methods give 2008-2009 to 2019-2020 seasons.",
  "practicalImplications":"Expect a substantial share of players with a hamstring injury to be reinjured, and build reinjury monitoring into rehabilitation and return-to-play planning. Team-level differences should prompt a review of prevention and treatment practices rather than be taken as proof of what works.",
  "athleteDev":"Track hamstring injury history in skill players, who were injured most often, and plan speed and change-of-direction exposure with reinjury risk in mind. Keep injury records consistent so team-level rates can be compared properly.",
  "rtp":"The average time on the injury report was 2.4 weeks, and previous injury was not linked to a longer absence. The study does not test return-to-play criteria or show that any return timing reduces reinjury, so it should not set return timelines on its own."
 }
}

{

 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text, 'Risk Associated with the Use of Selected Ingredients in Food Supplements', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains":["Nutrition & Hydration","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Nutrition","Sports Medicine","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of four newer food supplement categories: pre-workout, fat burner or thermogenic, brain or cognitive booster, and hormone or testosterone booster. The authors report contamination with unauthorized substances, ingredients that are medicines or synthetic compounds, and substances prohibited by WADA, and conclude that these categories carry the highest risk of harmful ingredients. The review cites survey prevalence data on supplement use in athletes, students and soldiers, but it does not report new outcome data.",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a narrative review with no described search method and no clinical outcome data in athletes. Much of the content is chemical, regulatory and doping-list material, and the ingredient selection was not systematic.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read this review as showing that these products harm athletes, when it is a safety and legality review without athlete outcome data.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2021,
  "citation":"Jędrejko K, Lazur J, Muszyńska B. Risk Associated with the Use of Selected Ingredients in Food Supplements. Chem Biodivers. 2021;18:e2000686.",
  "doi":"10.1002/cbdv.202000686",
  "abstract":"This review covers four newer categories of food supplements sold in Europe, the US, Australia and parts of Asia. It describes contamination, unauthorized and synthetic ingredients, and WADA-prohibited substances, and it links several ingredients to adverse effects and legal issues. The authors conclude that pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster products have the highest risk of harmful content.",
  "tldr":"Pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster supplements carry the highest risk of harmful or prohibited ingredients. Athletes should check products carefully before use, especially where doping rules apply.",
  "methods":"A narrative review of the chemical, regulatory and doping literature on selected supplement ingredients, with reference to EFSA novel food rules and WADA lists. No systematic search method is described.",
  "findings":"Products in the four categories may contain stimulants, plant ingredients used to disguise stimulants, medicines or synthetic compounds, and substances prohibited by WADA. Some products contain combinations of active ingredients that may cause adverse effects, and some have led to doping sanctions.",
  "limitations":"No systematic search method is described, and the review contains no athlete clinical outcome data. Prevalence figures come from heterogeneous surveys, and product contents vary by brand and batch.",
  "practicalImplications":"Athletes and staff should check pre-workout, fat burner and hormone-related products against WADA lists and be cautious about unlabelled stimulants. The review supports caution over these categories rather than proof of harm from any single product.",
  "athleteDev":"Athletes using pre-workout or fat-burning supplements should check ingredients against WADA lists and avoid products with undeclared stimulants or hormone-related compounds.",
  "rtp":"Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The review contains no rehabilitation or injury-recovery data."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review of 17 prospective studies across nine field-based team contact sports, from 4,012 records found in eight databases.  "screeningLimitations":"The pooled evidence rests on 17 studies with inconsistent injury definitions, diagnosis methods and incidence reporting, and only seven reported an incidence rate.   "citation":"Dolan P, Kenny I, Glynn L, Campbell M, Warrington GD, Cahalan R, et al. Risk Factors for Acute Ankle Sprains in Field-Based, Team Contact Sports: a Systematic Review of Prospective Etiological Studies. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2022.",
  "doi":"10.1080/00913847.2022.2093618",
  "abstract":"This systematic review identified prospectively measured ankle sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports. The authors suggest that BMI, ankle strength, hip strength and single-leg landing performance be considered in athlete assessment, and call for standardized injury definitions.",
  "tldr":"Ankle strength, hip strength, BMI and single-leg landing performance were linked to ankle sprain risk across team sports, but the evidence is thin and inconsistent. Use these measures in screening with awareness of the limits, and record injuries with standard definitions.",

  "findings":"Twelve risk factors were associated with ankle sprain incidence, including anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle, joint laxity, height, mass, BMI, age, ankle strength, hip strength, single-leg landing performance and single-leg reach.   "athleteDev":"Use ankle and hip strength tests and single-leg landing and reach screening as part of athlete assessment and program design, as the review proposes. Record injuries with standard definitions so findings can be checked locally.",

 "identityCheck":"Title in text, 'Risk Factors for Acute Ankle Sprains in Field-Based, Team Contact Sports: a Systematic Review of Prospective Etiological Studies', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Healthy Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review of 17 prospective studies across nine field-based team contact sports, from 4,012 records found in eight databases. The authors report that 12 of 20 risk-factor categories were associated with ankle sprain incidence, including ankle strength, hip strength, BMI, height, mass, single-leg landing performance and single-leg reach. Most of these associations came from only one or two studies, and injury definitions and diagnosis methods varied widely.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The pooled evidence rests on 17 studies with inconsistent injury definitions, diagnosis methods and incidence reporting, and only seven reported an incidence rate. Several associations come from single studies, and the BMI findings conflict, with one study reporting a protective effect.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the 12 associated factors as validated screening tests for ankle sprain, when most rest on one or two studies that used different definitions.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2022,
  "citation":"Dolan P, Kenny I, Glynn L, Campbell M, Warrington GD, Cahalan R, et al. Risk Factors for Acute Ankle Sprains in Field-Based, Team Contact Sports: a Systematic Review of Prospective Etiological Studies. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2022.",
  "doi":"10.1080/00913847.2022.2093618",
  "abstract":"This systematic review identified prospectively measured ankle sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports. Seventeen studies met the criteria, and 12 risk-factor categories were associated with ankle sprain incidence. The authors suggest that BMI, ankle strength, hip strength and single-leg landing performance be considered in athlete assessment, and call for standardized injury definitions.",
  "tldr":"Ankle strength, hip strength, BMI and single-leg landing performance were linked to ankle sprain risk across team sports, but the evidence is thin and inconsistent. Use these measures in screening with awareness of the limits, and record injuries with standard definitions.",
  "methods":"Eight databases were searched for prospective studies of ankle sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports. Study quality was rated with a modified CASP checklist, and data were extracted from the 17 included studies.",
  "findings":"Twelve risk factors were associated with ankle sprain incidence, including anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle, joint laxity, height, mass, BMI, age, ankle strength, hip strength, single-leg landing performance and single-leg reach. Deficits or asymmetries in ankle strength and hip strength were each associated in two studies.",
  "limitations":"Only the accepted author version was available, so pagination is missing. Injury definitions and diagnosis varied, and only seven of 17 studies reported an incidence rate. Several associations come from single studies, and the BMI findings conflict across studies.",
  "practicalImplications":"Ankle and hip strength, BMI and single-leg landing performance can be included in athlete assessment as the authors suggest, with the thin evidence base in mind. Measuring these in a standardized way across seasons would make results more useful.",
  "athleteDev":"Use ankle and hip strength tests and single-leg landing and reach screening as part of athlete assessment and program design, as the review proposes. Record injuries with standard definitions so findings can be checked locally.",
  "rtp":"The review concerns the risk of a first ankle sprain in healthy athletes. It does not inform return-to-play decisions after an ankle sprain."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q08", "sourceFile":"SOURCE_PLACEHOLDER", "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text, 'Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football: medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League clubs', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Observational study of chief medical officers from 15 European male professional football clubs, who suggested 21 modifiable hamstring risk factors and rated their importance on a 5-point scale. Seven clubs with below-average and eight with above-average hamstring injury burden in 2019/20 and 2020/21 were compared. The top-rated factors were lack of communication between medical and coaching staff (weighted average 3.7) and lack of regular high-speed football in training (3.6), and 12 of the 21 factors were extrinsic.",
 "screeningLimitations":"These are expert opinions about risk factors, not measured exposures, and the design cannot show cause. The sample is 15 clubs, injury burden groups were based on two seasons, and the authors note the findings may not generalize to other clubs.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the medical officers' rankings as evidence of which hamstring risk factors cause injury, when the study records what clinicians believe.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2023,
  "citation":"Ekstrand J, Ueblacker P, Van Zoest W, Verheijen R, Vanhecke B, et al. Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football: medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League clubs. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2023;9:e001461.",
  "doi":"10.1136/bmjsem-2022-001461",
  "abstract":"Chief medical officers of 15 European professional clubs suggested and rated hamstring injury risk factors. Most were extrinsic, linked to coaching, team or club. Clubs with higher hamstring injury burden rated fatigue, wellness and coach leadership style as more important than clubs with lower burden.",
  "tldr":"Club medical officers rate communication between medical and coaching staff and high-speed training exposure as the most important hamstring risk factors, and most of the factors they name are controlled by coaching staff. The study shows clinicians' beliefs, not proven causes.",
  "methods":"Chief medical officers of 15 clubs completed an online questionnaire. They first named risk factors, then rated each on a 5-point scale, and ratings were compared between clubs with lower and higher than average hamstring injury burden using weighted averages.",
  "findings":"Twenty-one risk factors were suggested, with 12 extrinsic and nine intrinsic. Compared with the low-burden group, the high-burden group rated fatigue (3.6 vs 2.6), player wellness (3.0 vs 2.0) and coach leadership style (3.3 vs 2.1) as more important. The low-burden group rated lack of high-speed training higher (3.8 vs 3.5).",
  "limitations":"Findings rest on expert opinion from 15 clubs, with only two seasons of injury data used to form the groups. The authors note the study design cannot show causality, and other club differences that were not measured may explain the injury rates.",
  "practicalImplications":"Clubs can review how medical and coaching staff communicate about load and fatigue, and how much high-speed running is included in training, since these were rated most important. The study does not show that changing these factors reduces hamstring injury.",
  "athleteDev":"Build regular high-speed running exposure into training, and manage load through joint decisions between coaching and medical staff, as the medical officers recommended. Monitor fatigue and player wellness, which the higher-burden clubs rated as more important.",
  "rtp":"Not applicable to return-to-play decisions, because the study covers risk factors for hamstring injury rather than recovery. It rates residual weakness after a previous hamstring injury as an important risk factor, but it does not test return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

587	3.3 Risk Factors for Ankle Sprain
588	Across the twelve studies, the following categories were investigated: age, sex, injury history,
589	sport, foot/leg dominance, athletic exposure, anthropometrics, general joint laxity, ankle
590	laxity, anatomical alignment, ankle and hip range of motion, ankle strength, calf strength,
591	center of gravity (balance or similar), muscle reaction time (perturbation), hip strength,
592	movement screens, power, body fat%, respiratory capacity, and flexibility.
593	
594	Table 3 presents mass, height, BMI and age as risk factors for ankle sprain from studies that
595	reported these findings. In addition to these anthropometric variables, six studies investigated
596	ankle stability by examining ligamentous laxity [61-63, 66, 67, 73]. The Modified Beighton
597	Method (general laxity) was used in two studies showing no differences between the injured
598	and uninjured groups [62, 63]. Joint laxity of the ankle using the anterior drawer test was
599	used in four studies [61-63, 67], where one study assessed with using an ankle arthrometer
600	and an ankle instability questionnaire [73], again all presenting no statistically significant
601	differences between groups. One study reported a general finding (no method reported) of
602	clinical instability of injured players’ ankles [66]. Arnason et al. [61], Baumhauer et al. [62],
603	and Beynnon et al. [63] also used a second ankle joint laxity test called the Talar Tilt Test,
604	which only Beynnon et al. [63] found a difference between the injured and uninjured groups

3.3 Risk Factors for Ankle Sprain
Across the twelve studies, the following categories were investigated: age, sex, injury history,
sport, foot/leg dominance, athletic exposure, anthropometrics, general joint laxity, ankle
laxity, anatomical alignment, ankle and hip range of motion, ankle strength, calf strength,
center of gravity (balance or similar), muscle reaction time (perturbation), hip strength,
movement screens, power, body fat%, respiratory capacity, and flexibility.

Table 3 presents mass, height, BMI and age as risk factors for ankle sprain from studies that
reported these findings. In addition to these anthropometric variables, six studies investigated
ankle stability by examining ligamentous laxity [61-63, 66, 67, 73]. The Modified Beighton
Method (general laxity) was used in two studies showing no differences between the injured
and uninjured groups [62, 63]. Joint laxity of the ankle using the anterior drawer test was
used in four studies [61-63, 67], where one study assessed with using an ankle arthrometer
and an ankle instability questionnaire [73], again all presenting no statistically significant
differences between groups. One study reported a general finding (no method reported) of
clinical instability of injured players’ ankles [66]. Arnason et al. [61], Baumhauer et al. [62],
and Beynnon et al. [63] also used a second ankle joint laxity test called the Talar Tilt Test,
which only Beynnon et al. [63] found a difference between the injured and uninjured groups
